planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring just below soil level with the crown at the surface, in humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this older, RHS Award of Garden Merit-winning hybrid is prized for its dependable vigor and rich winter leaf color.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, tugging off spent or tattered leaves each spring to keep the rosettes tidy. Sunningdale is one of the oldest and most garden-worthy Bergenia hybrids, forming a large, vigorous clump of broad, leathery leaves that flush deep copper-red through autumn and winter, especially where some winter sun reaches the foliage. In mid-spring, dense clusters of rose-pink flowers open from dark red calyces atop tall, bright red stems well above the leaves, giving strong color contrast against the bronzed foliage. Its size and toughness suit it to mass planting as a weed-suppressing groundcover beneath shrubs or along shaded pathways; divide congested clumps every four to five years in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this German-raised, RHS Award of Garden Merit hybrid is notable among bergenias for producing repeat flushes of bloom into summer and fall rather than flowering only once in spring.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, removing faded flower stems to encourage the later flushes of bloom this cultivar is known for. Morgenrote (Morning Red) bears trusses of rich rose-pink flowers on tall red stems above a raised rosette of large, glossy, deep-green leaves that take on plum tones in cool weather, and unlike most bergenias it continues to send up scattered new flower stems through summer and into autumn rather than blooming only once. This long, repeat-flowering season makes it one of the more valuable bergenias for sustained color at the front of a shaded border. Divide crowded clumps every four to five years in spring by cutting through the woody rhizomes.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown stock in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; unlike most bergenias this Himalayan species is deciduous, dying back after hard frost and re-emerging with fresh, hairy new leaves each spring.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, reliably moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh drying wind. Hairy bergenia is a Himalayan species distinguished from the more familiar B. cordifolia by its large, rounded leaves, which are softly covered on both surfaces with fine down and often flushed red as they emerge in early spring. Clusters of white flowers that age to soft pink open on red stalks in early spring, often ahead of the fully expanded foliage. It is markedly less cold-hardy and less evergreen than most garden bergenias - the leaves are damaged or killed by hard frost and the plant is deciduous in cold winters, so it suits milder, sheltered shade gardens best. Its softer, fuzzy-textured foliage offers a distinct contrast to the glossy leaves of other bergenia species and cultivars.
